_comment: The document installed copies read to find out whether anything newer exists.
Two things version independently: the app (a new installer) and the tune (the
sound itself, applied in place without a reinstall).
WHERE THIS IS SERVED FROM: dfzi/foresight-releases, a PUBLIC repository that
carries release artifacts only -- no source. The app fetches this file from its
main branch and the installer from its releases. Anonymous requests have to
succeed, which is why it cannot live beside the source.
THE APP HALF IS GENERATED. CI overwrites appVersion, appRevision,
appDownloadUrl and appSha256 when it publishes, so the copy in this repository
is a template and editing those four by hand achieves nothing. The tune half is
hand-authored, by the procedure below.
PUBLISHING A NEW TUNE:
1. Edit tune-pack.json, raise its "revision".
2. sha256sum tune-pack.json
3. Put that hash in tuneSha256 here and raise tuneRevision to match.
4. Publish both files to the host above.
The hash is not optional. An installed copy applies this to a stranger's audio
configuration without them reviewing it, so a truncated download or a
substituted file has to be refused rather than partially applied.
appSha256 is PUBLISHED BUT NOT YET ENFORCED. The app only ever shows
appDownloadUrl and opens it in a browser -- it never fetches and runs the
installer itself -- so there is nothing for a hash to guard yet. It is stamped
here so a user can verify a download by hand, and so the field already exists
when in-app installation lands. Whoever builds that must not treat the hash as
sufficient on its own: a tampered manifest simply carries a matching hash for a
malicious file. The check that actually closes it is Authenticode -- verifying
the installer is signed by us -- which needs a code-signing certificate first.
